Lessons.Title: The Shape of Distributions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: describe a distribution as symmetric, roughly bell-shaped, skewed, uniform or bimodal; defend the classification with evidence; and suggest a possible data-collection context without presenting the guess as fact. Independently authored Edulytiks lesson based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition, Unit 1 Lesson 4, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/4/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher role: Addressing HSS-ID.A.1; Building Towards HSS-ID.A.2.

Original data displays: at numerical values 1,2,3,4,5, data A have frequencies 1,2,4,2,1; B have 2,2,2,2,2; C have 5,3,1,1,1; D have 4,1,1,1,4. Use equally spaced values, draw one dot per observation and label each count. A is a roughly bell-shaped symmetric example, B uniform, C right-skewed and D bimodal. The data are fabricated specifically for mathematical practice, not attributed to actual students.

Partner matching task: compare the four dot plots and their frequency tables, name their shapes, and support each classification with two observations. Trade roles: the partner challenges a match or explains why it is valid. Invent a possible numerical survey question that might generate one display, then explain why a graph alone cannot prove which real survey was conducted.

Important distinctions: symmetry does not imply bell shape (a uniform display can be symmetric); a distribution's skew is named by the direction of its tail rather than the side containing its highest bar; two peaks may not represent two distinct populations. A box plot may conceal peaks that are obvious in a dot plot.

Teacher-scored rubric: give 0, 1 or 2 points each for accurate classification, numerical justification, plausible context with variable and units, and reasoned critique of partner claims (8 maximum). This is an explanation/card-matching activity, not a single machine-graded number. The first-party frequency tables are not publisher artwork.

KeyConcepts.Title: Symmetry and bell shape
KeyConcepts.Definition: A symmetric distribution has matching frequencies reflected around a center; a bell-shaped distribution has one central peak with frequencies tapering outward.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test mirrored pairs, then check for a central peak.
KeyConcepts.Example: Frequencies 1,2,4,2,1 are symmetric and roughly bell-shaped; 2,2,2,2,2 are symmetric and uniform.

KeyConcepts.Title: Skewness
KeyConcepts.Definition: A distribution is right-skewed when a sparse tail extends farther toward larger values, and left-skewed when the tail extends toward smaller values.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find the main cluster and the tail, not merely the tallest bar.
KeyConcepts.Example: Frequencies 5,3,1,1,1 over increasing values have a right tail.

KeyConcepts.Title: Uniform and bimodal
KeyConcepts.Definition: Uniform data have approximately equal frequencies across the shown values; bimodal data have two distinct common-value peaks.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read numerical counts at each peak and compare between-peak frequencies.

WorkedExamples.Title: Bell-shaped versus uniform
WorkedExamples.Question: Classify frequencies 1,2,4,2,1 across values 1 to 5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare pairs equally spaced from the central value and find the peak.
Steps: At 1 and 5 the counts both equal 1.
At 2 and 4 the counts both equal 2.
At the center 3 there are 4 observations, the single maximum.
The frequencies rise then fall symmetrically; the ten observations form a small roughly bell-shaped display.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Approximately bell-shaped and symmetric, not uniform.

WorkedExamples.Title: Direction of skew
WorkedExamples.Question: For values 1 through 5 with frequencies 5,3,1,1,1, where does the tail extend?
WorkedExamples.Method: Locate the bulk and follow sparse observations away from it.
Steps: Values 1 and 2 contain 8 of the 11 observations.
Sparse observations remain at 3,4,5, each larger than the cluster.
The tail points toward greater values, so it is right-skewed.
Compute the weighted mean (5*1+3*2+1*3+1*4+1*5)/11=23/11, and median is 2.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Right-skewed; mean 23/11 is slightly greater than median 2.
WorkedExamples.Check: The weighted sum equals 23 and there are 11 observations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Propose but do not assert a context
WorkedExamples.Question: What kind of variable might yield two frequency peaks at ratings 1 and 5?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the chart to suggest one hypothesis and distinguish speculation from data.
Steps: The two peaks show values 1 and 5 have count 4 each.
Values 2,3,4 occur once each, so the middle has fewer responses.
A possible interpretation is an anonymous 1–5 preference scale with polarized responses.
Other contexts can produce this shape, so the chart cannot establish what was actually surveyed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A bimodal rating pattern is plausible, but a source population or survey question cannot be inferred as a fact.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A uniform distribution can be symmetric while lacking one center peak.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the frequencies for a single tapering center, not only mirror pairs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Naming skew by the location of the tallest bar
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The tail, not the modal bar, determines the skew direction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the bulk then find which direction the sparse values extend.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a graph proves a real survey context
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Many data-generating processes can share the same shape.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label any explanation a hypothesis and propose an experiment to test it.

SummaryPoints: Describe data shapes using evidence from the actual frequencies and horizontal scales.
Symmetry, unimodality and bell shape are distinct properties; uniform data need not have a peak.
Skew direction follows the tail; bimodal means two distinct peaks.
Open context invention and partner critique require a teacher-scored rubric.
